newsitem.title: UK: Rushdie says EU "weakness" encourages Iran attacks.
newsitem.headline: Rushdie says EU "weakness" encourages Iran attacks.

text.p: British author Salman Rushdie, who lives under the shadow of an Iranian death threat, said Europe's "weakness" in the face of political killings ordered by Iran's government would encourage further deaths.
"The only message that can be deduced from the weakness of the European response is Go right ahead guys, do it again, we don't mind'," Rushdie said in a BBC interview due to be broadcast on Monday.
"If Iran were thinking of planning other assassinations in Europe of other dissidents or whoever it may be...they have been given carte blanche."

The European Union withdrew its ambassadors from Tehran in April after a German court ruled that Iran's leaders ordered the shooting of four Iranian Kurdish dissidents in Berlin, but decided three weeks later to allow the envoys to return.

"Europe has displayed a degree of cynicism that I would not have believed them capable of," Rushdie said. "That's to say what all this is about is not wanting to do anything to rock the boat of greed and money."

A death edict, or fatwa, on the Indian-born author was issued in 1989 by Iran's then spiritual leader Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini because of alleged blasphemy against Islam in his novel "The Satanic Verses".
Rushdie, who has lived in hiding ever since, said he had been told of attempts to kill him.
"There have been a number of occasions when I've been told that there have been efforts underway, I mean real, active, identified assassination attempts," he said.
